prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "MCDONALDS CORP" (ticker MCD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "MCD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: McDonald's Corporation

mission.statement: Our mission is to make delicious feel-good moments easy for everyone.
mission.source: McDonald's corporate website, 'Our Mission and Values' page
mission.plain: McDonald's wants to make it quick and easy for anyone to get tasty food that makes them happy.

about.plain: McDonald's is the world's biggest burger chain, selling Big Macs, fries, Chicken McNuggets, breakfast and drinks. It has more than 45,000 restaurants in over 100 countries. About 95% of them are run by local business owners who pay McDonald's rent and a share of their sales. McDonald's often owns or leases the land and buildings, so it is partly a landlord too.
about.customers: Everyday people and families who want cheap, fast and familiar food, through the drive-thru, counter, app or delivery.
about.everyday: The Golden Arches, the Happy Meal and the Big Mac are known almost everywhere in the world.

money.part: Rent and fees from franchised restaurants
money.plain: rent, royalties and initial fees from owners
fees for tech platforms and licensed products

money.part: Loyalty, digital and AI-run restaurant platform
money.plain: app ordering, loyalty, ArchIQ and drive-thru voice AI

result.summary: McDonald's has a wide moat built on one of the world's most recognised brands, unmatched scale in buying, marketing and real estate, and a franchise system where more than 45,000 restaurants pay it rent and royalties. Its operating margin was 46.1% in 2025, far above restaurant peers, but traffic has weakened as lower-income customers pushed back on prices, showing the moat protects profits better than it protects volumes.

pricingPower.evidence: McDonald's USA said in May 2024 that the average menu item cost about 40% more than in 2019, and the price rises lifted sales for years; but lower-income guests then cut visits, forcing the $5 Meal Deal (2024) and value menus, and U.S. comparable sales rose only 0.8% in Q2 2026 against 2.5% a year earlier.

moats.evidence: The Golden Arches, Big Mac, Happy Meal and McCafé are among the most recognised brands on earth; the company says it serves more than 70 million customers a day and has 17 brands with at least $1 billion in annual sales.
Customers can switch to another chain at no cost; nearly 220 million active loyalty members (as of June 30, 2026) add only mild stickiness, though franchisees face high costs to leave the system.
More restaurants make the brand more convenient and spread advertising costs, and the loyalty app gains data, but one customer's use does not make the product better for another.

Systemwide sales of about $37 billion in Q2 2026 alone give it unmatched buying power for beef, potatoes and packaging, the biggest marketing budget in fast food, and spread technology costs such as the Google-backed AI ordering across the whole system.
It holds many of the best drive-thru corners and highway locations, often owning the land, which makes those sites hard for rivals to replicate.
Its franchise and real estate model is widely copied, so it does not rely on a model rivals refuse to adopt.

Decades of standardised kitchen operations, supply chain partners and franchisee training (Hamburger University) deliver consistent food at huge volume, though execution slipped in 2025-26 with uneven value-menu rollout.
Its owned and long-leased restaurant real estate (net property and equipment of $28,479M at June 30, 2026) is a rare portfolio of prime sites that earns rent from franchisees.

customers.evidence: It is one of the most visited restaurant brands with nearly 220 million active loyalty members, but it usually ranks near the bottom of the American Customer Satisfaction Index for fast food and lost lower-income traffic after price rises.

talent.evidence: Crew jobs are mostly entry-level hourly roles with high turnover in a franchised system; McDonald's is a famous first employer but does not appear among top 'best places to work' rankings, and the Sept 2026 NEXT plan includes its largest-ever workforce reskilling programme.

product.evidence: Its fries, Big Mac and McNuggets are iconic and consistent everywhere, but the food is not judged best-in-class on quality, and Chick-fil-A and better-burger chains often win taste and service surveys.

competitors.name: Restaurant Brands International (Burger King, Tim Hortons, Popeyes, Firehouse Subs)
competitors.note: Burger King is the most direct global burger rival; Popeyes in chicken and Tim Hortons in breakfast and coffee.

competitors.name: Yum! Brands (KFC, Taco Bell, Pizza Hut)
competitors.note: KFC competes worldwide in chicken and Taco Bell in US value fast food.

competitors.name: Chick-fil-A
competitors.note: Private US chicken chain with very high sales per restaurant, the main threat to McDonald's in chicken and drive-thru.

competitors.name: The Wendy's Company
competitors.note: US burger and breakfast rival competing heavily on value deals.

competitors.name: Inspire Brands (Arby's, Sonic, Dunkin', Jimmy John's)
competitors.note: Private group; Sonic in drive-thru burgers and Dunkin' in breakfast and coffee.

competitors.name: Starbucks
competitors.note: Coffee and breakfast occasions where McCafé competes.

competitors.name: Subway
competitors.note: Private global sandwich chain competing for quick lunches.

competitors.name: Chipotle Mexican Grill
competitors.note: Fast-casual rival taking younger and higher-income lunch and dinner visits.

competitors.name: Domino's Pizza
competitors.note: Competes for value meals and delivery orders.

competitors.name: Yum China (KFC and Pizza Hut in China)
competitors.note: Largest Western-style restaurant operator in China, where McDonald's is a minority-stake licensed brand.

competitors.name: Jack in the Box
competitors.note: Regional US burger chain in the West and South.

competitors.name: Jollibee Foods
competitors.note: Leads fast food in the Philippines and is expanding in Asia and North America.

competitors.name: Brinker International (Chili's)
competitors.note: Casual dining chain whose value bundles priced close to fast food have taken visits.

competitors.name: Dutch Bros
competitors.note: Drive-thru drinks chain popular with Gen Z, competing in the beverage push.

threats: Lower- and middle-income customers cutting fast-food visits after years of menu price rises (U.S. comparable sales only +0.8% in Q2 2026)
Chick-fil-A and other chicken chains winning share in the fastest-growing protein
Casual-dining and rival value bundles (Chili's, Burger King, Wendy's, Taco Bell) undercutting its value message
Beef costs near record highs with the U.S. cattle herd at multi-decade lows
GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and healthier eating trends reducing fast-food demand
Franchisee strain from value deals, wage laws (e.g. California's $20 fast-food minimum wage) and NEXT remodel costs
High debt ($39,863M at June 30, 2026) and negative shareholders' equity limiting flexibility if rates rise
Food-safety incidents such as the October 2024 E. coli outbreak linked to Quarter Pounder onions

ceo.name: Chris Kempczinski
ceo.background: Duke University BA, Harvard MBA; Procter & Gamble brand manager, Boston Consulting Group consultant, PepsiCo and Kraft Foods executive; McDonald's USA president 2016-2019; chairman since 2024

c1.evidence: McDonald's leads global fast food, but the industry is mature: 2025 revenue grew 3.7% to $26,885M and global comparable sales rose only 1.3% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Customers pick it for convenience, speed, familiar taste and value at more than 45,000 locations, and its brand, scale and prime real estate are very hard to copy, though value perception has weakened.

c3.evidence: The Golden Arches are recognised almost everywhere and McDonald's is the default fast-food chain, though customer recommendation is middling given its low American Customer Satisfaction Index scores.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to make delicious feel-good moments easy for everyone' is published but rarely leads the story, and management is mainly driven by sales, margins and shareholder returns.

c6.evidence: “cheap, fast, convenient, unhealthy” - the impression is familiar and mixed: people value speed and consistency but associate it with junk food and, lately, rising prices.

c7.evidence: Global eating-out spending is huge and grows steadily, but it does not ride a fast secular trend; McDonald's expects new restaurants to add about 2.5% to systemwide sales growth in 2027, moderating to about 2% by 2030.

c8.evidence: Its NEXT plan targets 1.5 percentage points of share gains in chicken and beverages by 2030, but it stays within fast food and has exited concepts like CosMc's.

m1.evidence: Kempczinski has a clear plan (Accelerating the Arches, then McDonald's > NEXT through 2036 with AI-enabled ArchIQ and $8.5B of franchisee support), but it is an operating plan rather than a bold vision of the future.

m2.evidence: He is a professional manager who joined in 2015 from Kraft, not a founder, although the 10-year NEXT plan shows long-term thinking.

m4.evidence: He talks about franchisee economics and customer value and the NEXT plan funds rent relief and remodels, but his 2021 texts to Chicago's mayor drew criticism and crew pay remains a sore point.

m5.evidence: He pushed a 'more professional culture' and a faster, digital-first organisation, but menu innovation is incremental (Big Arch, new drinks, hand-breaded chicken).

m6.evidence: He has led the digital, loyalty and Google AI drive-thru work, but his background is brand management, consulting and strategy rather than engineering.

m7.evidence: He led the 2022 exit from Russia (853 restaurants, about 62,000 staff kept paid until the sale) but also apologised in 2021 for texts blaming parents of children killed by gun violence in Chicago.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Chris Kempczinski at Stanford, Harvard, MIT or another top university could be found.

m8b.evidence: He is a disciplined, low-key corporate executive; his March 2026 Big Arch promo video was mocked as stiff and corporate.

m9.evidence: Under him revenue rose from $19,208M (2020) to $26,885M (2025) and operating income from $7,324M to $12,393M, but U.S. traffic and comparable sales weakened in 2025-26 and the shares fell from about $306 at end-2025 to $242.97 by Oct 16, 2026.

m10.evidence: McDonald's runs a lean, cost-focused franchise model and targets G&A of about 1.9% of systemwide sales by 2030, but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: It feeds more than 70 million people a day with affordable, safe and consistent food worldwide, but it is a convenience rather than a life-changing product.

p2.evidence: Running a consistent food system at 45,000+ restaurants is operationally hard, but making burgers and fries is not technically hard or critical to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in four of the last five years (2021 $23,223M, 2023 $25,494M, 2024 $25,920M, 2025 $26,885M), dipping only slightly in 2022 to $23,183M.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 38.1% in 2020 to 46.1% in 2025 (with a dip to 40.4% in 2022), but McDonald's does not report a gross margin.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had $39,863M of long-term debt against $822M of cash and shareholders' equity of -$1,023M, although 2025 operating cash flow of $10,551M covers debt service easily.

f4.evidence: Operating income grew from $7,324M (2020) to $12,393M (2025) and operating cash flow from $6,265M to $10,551M, with dips in 2022 and 2024.

v1.evidence: It is the most convenient and familiar choice, but rivals such as Chick-fil-A (service, chicken) or Chipotle (fresher food) are often judged better on quality.

v2.evidence: McDonald's is a well-known first job but does not appear among the top 'best places to work' rankings, and fast-food crew work is mostly low-paid with high turnover.

c5.evidence: Hundreds of millions of people, plus thousands of franchisees and their staff, would miss a cheap, quick and reliable meal, but its food also draws criticism for its health effects.
